articles.title: Your showcase

body.support:
This is your big talk. It is three to five minutes long.

**Pick a topic.** Choose something real.
- how to enrol to vote.
- how to get your learner permit.
- how to rent your first place.
- why people should give blood or volunteer.

**Decide your purpose.**
- To **inform**: give facts.
- To **instruct**: show how to do it.
- To **advocate**: get people to act.
.
**Plan it.**
- Hook.
- Say what’s coming.
- Two or three points.
- Wrap-up.

**Back it up.** Use two or three facts. Say where they came from.

**Practise.** Out loud. Time it. Film it.

**On the day:**
- Slow down. Look up. Stand still.
- Take questions.
.
**After:** watch your video. What went well? What would you change?
body.core:
This is your showcase: a three-to-five-minute presentation on something that matters in everyday life or your community.

**1. Choose a topic and purpose.** Topics could include enrolling to vote, getting your licence, renting, Medicare, a first job, giving blood, volunteering, or joining a community group. Then decide your purpose:
- **inform:** explain what it is and why it matters.
- **instruct:** show the audience how to do it, step by step.
- **advocate:** persuade them to act.

Many talks do two of these. Inform first, then advocate.

**2. Know your audience.** What do they know already? What do they care about? Choose examples from their world.

**3. Structure it.** Hook, preview, two or three main points with signposts, wrap-up with a call to action.

**4. Back it.** Use two or three pieces of evidence from reliable sources, credited out loud (“According to the Australian Electoral Commission…”). Use logic, reasoning and emotion: a fact, a “because… so…”, a short story.

**5. Visual aids.** Optional, but useful. If you use slides: one idea per slide, a picture and a few words, and credit images. Face the room, not the screen. A real object, like an enrolment form, can work better than slides.

**6. Rehearse.** Out loud, timed and recorded, at least three times. Mark up your cue cards.

**7. Deliver and take questions.** Slow down, pause, look up, stand still. Listen, repeat, answer, check.

**8. Evaluate.** Watch the recording. Use the rubric. Name specific moments. Set a target.
body.extend:
Your showcase is a three-to-five-minute talk. It **informs**, **instructs** or **advocates** on taking part in your community (**civic** life) or managing everyday life.

**Purpose and topic.** Choose a topic with real value for your audience. Ideas: enrolling to vote, getting a licence, renting, health services, rights at work, volunteering or giving blood. Decide your main purpose. Strong talks often combine them: inform, then instruct, then advocate.

**Audience.** Think about what they know and care about. Choose examples, words and your mix of logic, reasoning and emotion to suit.

**Structure.** Hook, preview, main points linked by signposts, and a wrap-up with a clear call to action. Pick an order that fits: steps for instructions, problem then solution for advocacy.

**Evidence and credit.** Use reliable, current evidence. Credit it out loud to build **credibility**. Add a reference list. Credit and clear any images, music or video.

**Visual aids.** Use slides or objects only where they add meaning. Few words, strong images, one idea each. Never read your slides.

**Delivery.** Control your pace, pauses, intonation, eye contact, stance and gestures. Handle questions with active listening, rephrasing and honest answers.

**Judge your own work.** Watch a recording against the rubric. Name exact moments. Find causes, not just symptoms. For example: “I rushed point 2 because I hadn’t practised the link.” Then set one or two targets.

caseStudies.title: “Be proud of who you are”

body.support:
**Dylan Alcott** is a champion athlete. He won gold medals in wheelchair tennis and basketball.

In **January 2022**, he was named **Australian of the Year**. He was the first person with a disability to win it.

He gave a speech. He told the truth about his life. He said that as a kid, he hated having a disability.

Then he spoke to young people with disability. He told them to be proud of who they are.

He also asked the government for help for people with disability.

His speech used a true story and a clear ask. Lots of people heard it.
body.core:
**Dylan Alcott** has won Paralympic gold medals in wheelchair tennis and wheelchair basketball.

In **January 2022**, he was named **Australian of the Year**. He was the first person with a disability to win the award.

In his speech, he was honest. He said that as a kid, he hated having a disability. He didn’t want to be different. That true story made people listen.

Then he spoke to young people with disability. He told them to be proud of who they are.

He also made clear **asks** of the government. He asked for secure funding for the **NDIS**, the scheme that supports people with disability. He also asked for free COVID tests for people with disability.

The speech went from a story, to a message, to action. That’s a strong plan for any talk that tries to change things.
body.extend:
**Dylan Alcott** has won Paralympic gold in wheelchair tennis and wheelchair basketball. In **January 2022**, he was named **Australian of the Year**. He was the first person with a disability to receive the award.

His speech is a strong model of **civic** advocacy. It opened with humour. Then it turned personal. He said he hated his disability as a child and didn’t want to be different. Sharing that built trust, or **credibility**, and made people feel for him.

Next, he spoke straight to one audience: young people with disability. He urged them to be proud of who they are.

Finally, he made clear asks of the government. He wanted guaranteed funding for the **National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS)**. He also wanted free rapid COVID tests for people with disability.

The speech moved from personal story (emotion), to message (reasons for inclusion), to action. Different audiences heard different things. Young people heard hope. Governments heard a request.

Reports of his exact words vary a little. Check a full recording before you quote him.

model.text:
**Opening:** “Hands up if you’re 17. [pause] You can enrol to vote today, on your phone. I’ll show you what it is, how to do it, and why it matters.”
**Point 1:** “First, what is it? According to the Australian Electoral Commission, you can enrol from 16. You can vote from 18.”
**Self-evaluation:** My hook worked. People put their hands up. I rushed point 2. I hadn’t practised using the form while I talked. Someone asked about moving house. I answered, then checked: “Does that help?”
**My target:** rehearse with the form open, and slow down in point 2.
why: The opening hooks, previews and promises a clear map in three short lines.
The evidence is credited to an official source, out loud.
The evaluation names a cause (“hadn’t practised”) and a specific target.

rubric.good: Names what went well and what to fix.
rubric.great: Names causes and sets clear targets.

teacher.overview: The Speak Up boss mission and the VM Unit 4 Outcome 2 showcase. Students plan and deliver a three-to-five-minute presentation that informs, instructs or advocates on civic participation or managing everyday life (e.g. enrolling to vote, licensing, renting, Medicare, volunteering, blood donation). It draws together audience, structure, evidence and attribution, delivery and question handling, followed by critical self-evaluation from a recording. The case study is Dylan Alcott’s 2022 Australian of the Year speech, which moved from personal story to message to specific policy asks.
prep: Book presentation time (about 6 minutes per student including questions).
Students should have done at least two of Know Your Audience, Plan Your Talk, Back Your Advice and Nail the Delivery.
Consider inviting a real audience (another class, parents, a community member).

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Topic and purpose
steps: **Hook (5 min):** what’s one adult task nobody taught you?

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Rehearse
steps: **Rehearse (50 min):** three timed runs in pairs, with peer feedback; mark up cue cards; prepare visual aids.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Showcase
steps: **Do it (40 min):** presentations and questions (may need a second session).
**Evaluate (10 min):** start the evaluation; finish from the recording.

keyPoints: Real topic, clear purpose: inform, instruct or advocate.
Audience shapes examples, words and the logic–emotion mix.
Hook, preview, signposted points, wrap-up with a call to action.
Credited evidence and a reference list.
Rehearse, deliver, take questions, evaluate with causes and targets.

support: A plan frame and a list of trusted sites.
extend: Critical evaluation identifying causes and two targets.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 hook addressing the audience; 2 preview; 3 credited evidence (inform); 4 step-by-step (instruct); 5 personal story (advocate, emotion); 6 call to action; 7 reference.

**Sort:** inform — Medicare coverage; preferential voting. Instruct — learner permit steps; reading a lease. Advocate — give blood; youth space.

**Case study:** Alcott (Paralympic gold medallist) was named Australian of the Year in January 2022, the first person with a disability to receive it; he spoke about hating his disability as a child; urged young people with disability to be proud; asked for guaranteed NDIS funding and free rapid antigen tests for people with disability. Structure: story → message → action.

**Note:** check the AEC enrolment ages in the diagram (enrol from 16, vote from 18) against aec.gov.au before teaching.

realityCheck: **This is the big one.** Some students will be very anxious. Offer the recorded option, a smaller audience, or presenting in pairs with clear individual sections.
**Topics should be useful, not just interesting.** Steer students towards something their audience will actually do.
**The case study involves disability and personal disclosure.** Keep the focus on how the speech works.
**Works in a real class:** yes, especially with a real audience; younger students asking questions raises the stakes in a good way.
